## Executive Summary

Most teams running LLM agents in production still don't evaluate them automatically. The two 2026 surveys I found put that figure at **48% to 62%**, depending on who was asked. Even teams that do run evals mostly score only the final answer, not the steps the agent took to get there (its trajectory). Their LLM judges are rarely checked against human labels, and their test sets are too small to tell a good agent from a mediocre one. One caveat matters a lot: **the evidence rests on just two independent surveys**, and several key numbers come from only one of them.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is low, but the exact figure depends on the sample.** AIQ Report found that 62% of teams run no automated agent evaluation and rely on manual spot checks instead. That's 1,204 teams of all sizes, surveyed Jan–Feb 2026 ([AIQ Report, 2026-03-12](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). TechWire found 48% across 890 organisations with more than 200 employees ([TechWire, 2026-06-02](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)).
  - ⚠️ **Conflict between sources:** TechWire calls its 48% "down from" AIQ's 62%. But the two surveys covered different populations, and TechWire itself says the gap is "partly methodological" because smaller teams are less likely to evaluate. **This is not evidence of a 14-point improvement between March and June.** It's two snapshots of different groups.
  - AIQ's respondents chose to take part, recruited through practitioner newsletters. AIQ says this probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation, so the real share with no evals is likely *higher* than 62% ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)).
- **Teams mostly score outcomes, rarely trajectories.** AIQ: 24% score outcomes only and 9% score trajectory plus final answer. TechWire: 13% score trajectories. Both agree that trajectory scoring is rare and slowly growing ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals); [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)).
- **LLM judges are mostly unchecked.** Only 11% of teams using an LLM as a judge have checked its scores against human labels. The rest treat judge scores as ground truth ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). `[SINGLE SOURCE]`
- **Test sets are too small.** The median "golden set" (a fixed set of tasks with known good answers) has 22 tasks. AIQ says that's too few to separate a good agent from a mediocre one with any useful confidence ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). `[SINGLE SOURCE]`
- **The tooling market is small but projected to grow fast.** Northgate Analytics estimates $310M in 2025 and $2.4bn–$4.1bn by 2030. The spread depends on whether eval tools get absorbed into existing observability products or stay a separate category ([Northgate, 2026-07-15](https://northgate-analytics.example/notes/agent-eval-market-sizing)). `[PAYWALLED: only the abstract was available; the method and segment breakdown were not checked]`

## Detailed Analysis

### Adoption: the two surveys side by side

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 2026-03-12 (~8 months old, past the 6-month freshness window) | 2026-06-02 (~5 months old) |
| Sample | 1,204 teams, all sizes, self-selected through newsletters | 890 orgs, >200 employees |
| No automated eval | **62%** | **48%** |
| Trajectory scoring | 9% | 13% |
| Outcome-only scoring | 24% | not reported |
| Judge checked against human labels | 11% | not reported |
| Median golden set size | 22 tasks | not reported |

AIQ's three categories add up to 95%. The report doesn't say what the other ~5% do.

### What teams actually score (rough maturity ladder, from AIQ)

1. **Manual spot checks before release:** ~62%
2. **Automated scoring of final outcomes only:** ~24%
3. **Automated scoring of outcomes plus trajectory:** ~9% (13% in TechWire's larger-company sample)

Neither survey breaks down *which* outcome metrics teams use (task success, cost, latency, safety, etc.). **That's a gap in the evidence**, so I can't give you a reliable answer on it.

### Where the gaps are

| Gap | Why it matters | Evidence strength |
|---|---|---|
| No automated evals at all | Regressions reach users unnoticed | Medium: two sources agree on direction, not on size |
| Final answer only, no trajectory | An agent can get the right answer through unsafe, expensive or lucky steps | Medium: two sources |
| LLM judges never checked against humans | Judge scores may be confidently wrong | Low: one source |
| Golden sets too small (median 22) | Score changes are statistically noise | Low: one source |

### Sources I excluded

- **"The 17 Best Agent Evaluation Platforms in 2026" (top-ai-tools-daily):** I didn't cite this. The article says it was generated with AI assistance and contains affiliate links. Its claims also failed checking:
  - **"91% of AI agents fail once deployed to production"** has no source. **Don't repeat this figure.**
  - **"EvalTools charges $199/month"** is contradicted by EvalTools' own pricing page: Starter is €0, Team €249/month, Enterprise from €1,800/month ([evaltools.io/pricing](https://evaltools.io/pricing), updated 2026-05-20).
  - **"EvalTools has $40M ARR and 12,000+ enterprise customers"** is unverified and unlikely. EvalTools describes itself as a 31-person company serving mid-market SaaS teams ([evaltools.io/about](https://evaltools.io/about)).
- **EvalTools pages:** I used these only for facts about EvalTools itself. They're a vendor's own pages, not evidence about the market.

### Limits of this brief

The search kept returning the same small set of sources. I found no peer-reviewed work, no 2026 data from big analyst firms, and no survey fielded after June 2026. All numbers here should be treated as directional.

|---|---|---|
